..
Sunday-Tuesday: Mild and dry conditions start off the new week.
A ridge will be over the region Sunday with mostly clear skies 
then begin to flatten Monday and Tuesday as a broad upper-level 
trough expands toward the WA Coast and sends impulses across 
southern British Columbia. Skies will largely remain mostly 
sunny but Monday and Tuesday will feature bands of high clouds 
associated with the decaying upper-level fronts. Temperatures 
will warm another 1-2 degrees Sunday and further Monday before a
gently cooling trend on Tuesday. Despite the flattening ridge 
on Monday, the air mass actually warms in response to the upper-
low that has been spinning south of Lewiston departing which 
has been blocking the warmth from the south from expanding 
northward. Overall, weather impacts will be low with minor 
heatrisk the main concern in the afternoon as temperatures climb
into the 80s, roughly 10 degrees above normal. Nights will 
continue to offer relief with overnight lows dipping into the 
40s to lower 50s. Winds will remain light Sunday with speeds 
generally under 10 mph. The exception will be localized 
southerly winds near 10 mph and gusts 15-20 mph in the upper 
Okanogan Valley. By Monday, the evening sun-downer winds will 
increase from the west and northwest through the Cascade river 
valleys as the pressure gradient begins to tighten. Winds for 
Tuesday will become a bit more breezy region-wide as cooler air 
begins to bleed into the region. West to southwest winds will 
increase closer to 10-15 mph with gusts up to 20 mph and locally
25 mph through the Cascade gaps. Definitely not anomalous by 
any means but noticeably more wind vs Sunday and Monday. Models 
are in good agreement through this period.

Wednesday-weekend: The broad trough will have carved into the 
region by Wednesday with temperatures cooling further and 
residual breeziness. A reinforcing shot of cooler air and 
shortwave dropping into the offshore trough on Thursday will dig
into the base of the trough allowing flow to buckle slightly 
over the Inland NW. 70% of the ensemble solutions indicate a 
slight warming trend Thursday before the cooler fall-like trough
swings inland Friday into the weekend. Models look to be coming
into good agreement for this pattern evolution with the main 
differences coming with the precise arrival of the main cold 
front (Friday morning or Friday evening) but generally on 
Friday. The main trough will pass through Saturday and leave a 
broad trough and cool air mass in place for Sunday. 

As for impacts: Winds on Friday, Cooler temperatures, 
particularly in the mountains with high elevations near 
freezing, and increased chances for precipitation Friday-
Saturday with high elevation snow. 

Friday looks to be a windy day across the region with potential 
for sustained west to southwest winds around 15 mph and gusts 
20-30 mph. There is a 50-70% chance for wind gusts greater than 
20 mph and 20-40% for gusts to exceed 30 mph. This is to be 
expected with the air mass cooling as 850mb temperatures drop 
from near 14C Thursday to 6C Friday in the post frontal air 
mass. This will knock lowland high temperatures back into the 
60s by the weekend. As for precipitation, ensembles are 
indicating a 50% chance for at least 0.10" along the Cascade 
Crest and mountains of NE WA and N ID. The potential outcomes 
for these areas is as high as 0.60 inches which could equate to 
several inches of snow for those venturing into the high 
country. Confidence is much lower for rainfall amounts outside 
of these areas and will depend how progressive the Friday-
Saturday wave is. A slower solution could result in rainfall 
amounts in excess of 0.10" across much of Idaho and far eastern 
reaches of WA...a faster solution would deliver less than a 
tenth to most areas outside the Cascade Crest and Selkirks. Stay
tuned. /sb
